speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not rise immediately in my place because I thought the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) was rising once again on one of his numerous points of order, questions of privilege and the type of question that he raises on all matters. I felt that, with due deference, I would give him first chance to have a crack at whatever he wanted to say.
It gives me great pleasure to open debate today on Bill C-62 which would amend the Old Age Security Act and repeal the Old Age Assistance Act as well as amending all related acts. As hon. members are aware, the main feature of this bill is to provide income-tested allowances to spouses aged 60 to 64 of old age security recipients, to become effective October 1 of this year. This measure, which was announced in the Speech from the Throne of
Old Age Security Act
this thirtieth parliament, will permit the government to pay a monthly allowance to some 65,000 to 90,000 spouses of old age security pensioners who are in the most need of income.
Such a step, Madam Speaker, is in the tradition which Liberal governments have established in their treatment of our senior citizens and I should like to outline briefly the steps which have led to this latest measure. Since 1927, when parliament approved the old age pension act under which the federal government paid 50 per cent of the cost of a means-tested pension administered by the provinces, the improvements have been such that the federal government has assumed total responsibility for old age pensions. The means test gave way, on the recommendation of the 1950 joint parliamentary committee, to a universal flat-rate type of pension with eligibility based solely on age and residence. The same criteria remain in force today.
The next fundamental step was the establishment, in 1966, of the guaranteed income supplement, which was initially intended to be a transitional program for those who had little or no opportunity to participate in the Canada or Quebec pension plans established at the same time. In 1970, however, it was converted to a continuing program to guarantee a minimum level of income to Canada's pensioners. Such a move, Madam Speaker, is in keeping with a traditional value in our society which couples a benefit of right with a supplemental payment for those who most need it.
Two years later, in 1968, both the OAS and GIS payments were increased annually, with a 2 per cent ceiling accounting for rises in the consumer price index; the ceiling was removed in May, 1972, to allow for full escalation. As most members are aware, such escalation was changed to a quarterly base in October of 1973 to allow for even more rapid response to changes in the consumer price index on behalf of our senior citizens.
A short look back to 1967, when the GIS payments began, shows that the basic pension was then $75 per month, with a supplement of $30. The figures for July of this year stand at $125.76 for the basic pension, with a GIS of $88.21 for single pensioners giving a total per month of $213.97; and a GIS of $78.34 each at the married rate, giving a total income of $408 per month for a couple. It does not require much of a mathematician, Madam Speaker, to see that in those eight years the guaranteed minimum payment for Canada's pensioners has doubled and is now payable at age 65 rather than 68 as was the case in 1967.
The bill which is before us today represents one more fundamental step in improving the income security of Canada's old age security recipients. The plight of a couple, one of whom receives the old age pension and one who does not, is often brought to our attention. The spouse is, in most cases, not a member of the work force and highly unlikely to be employed in any case. Indeed, in these days of a call for earlier retirement, about which many serious reservations have been expressed, it can and does happen that employees are retired from work earlier than they would choose and when they could still have years of productive work ahead of them.
We tend to forget, Madam Speaker, that while the professional person-the doctor, dentist, lawyer, etc.-can choose his retirement age, those on salary or wages, usual-

June 6, 1975
Old Age Security Act
ly considerably less than those of the professional, are retired at an age to be specified by a union, employer or other outside and totally arbitrary force. Such cases can and do present hardships and it is for this reason that the Liberal Party, during the 1974 election campaign, committed itself to easing the burden on such couples by instituting this income-tested allowance for spouses in order to provide for those who most need it in our society a monthly income which would allow them to live in the dignity which they deserve.
I repeat, this measure is aimed at the couple which, at present, is expected to live on the pension of one. It does all that, but nothing more and in that sense is an interim measure. Indeed, I should like to assure hon. members that the others in the same age group, such as widowed, divorced or single people, are not forgotten in the light of measures outlined in the bill we are debating today.
I have been engaged, since April of 1973, in a review of Canada's social security plans and programs with my provincial counterparts. Basic propositions of that review read as follows:
That a guaranteed income should be available to people whose incomes are insufficient because they are unable to or are not expected to work and that the incomes of those who are working but whose incomes are inadequate should be supplemented under a single, general income supplementation plan with built-in work incentives.
These were propositions Nos. 6 and 7 of the working document tabled in this House in April, 1973.

I alluded previously to the income support and supplement program. In February 1975, the federal and provincial ministers of welfare reached an agreement on a twofold program, that is income support and income supplement. Income support applies to all persons who are unable to work, who should not work, or who cannot find employment under provincial labour standards.
The income supplement would extend to persons who work but whose income is inadequate for a number of reasons. My officials are in the process of drawing up the mode of application of the income support and supplement programs. Those procedures will be studied at the next federal and provincial welfare ministers' conference. It is hoped that shortly thereafter, the federal and provincial governments can reach an agreement, and that an income support program can be implemented sometime next year.
I would point out that, in the meantime, the needy who are not eligible for the spouse's allowance can get financial assistance through provincial and municipal welfare programs. The federal government shares half the cost of those programs through the Canada Pension Plan. I wish to point out another important factor: the introduction of the spouse's allowance should result in the elimination of a number of welfare cases and thus enable the provinces to save money that can then be applied to other areas of welfare.
1 would like now to take a few moments of the time of the House to outline the provisions of this measure as well as to explain briefly the other provisions of Bill C-62. As I have already mentioned, the basic pension and the supple-

ment for the spouse aged 60 to 64 will all be subject to an income test, the same test as is now applied to the GIS portion of pensions now payable. This will ensure that payments go to those who most need them, and are not granted on a universal basis. We estimate that this plan will provide a further $100 million in benefits to older Canadians and I am sure that the Canadian people would not expect us to do less. The pensions will be paid individually to each recipient; that is, the spouse who is not a pensioner will receive a cheque each month in his or her own right. Proof of age and residence will be required from the spouse, just as in the case of persons aged 65 and over, and proof of marital status will also be required.
In order to ensure consistency in federal programs, the same criteria which now apply to common law couples under the old age security and Canada Pension Plan will be used in the case of the spouse's allowance. That is, couples who have been living together in a common law relationship and publicly representing themselves as man and wife will be accepted, though the relationship must have lasted for a minimum period of one year on the last day of the preceding fiscal year if neither partner has a legal spouse, or three years if either partner has a legal spouse. My department will be sending application forms for this spouse's allowance in time for the program to come into effect on October 1, and therefore the onus is not on the pensioner or spouse to seek out such forms.
Turning now to the other provisions of the bill, Madam Speaker, I am particularly pleased to be able to introduce at this time a bill which seeks to authorize the governor in council to make a regulation whereby certain periods of absence from Canada can be counted as presence in Canada in determining eligibility for old age security. As hon. members know, "residence" and "presence in Canada" are not identical in the regulations of the Old Age Security Act and because of this some people have been penalized because of absences from Canada while serving in the Canadian armed forces, while employed by the federal or provincial governments, or while engaged as a missionary, for example. Some such cases have been brought to my attention, and hon. members may remember that on January 10, 1974, I gave a commitment in this House that power to make such a regulation would be sought from the House. We agree that it is untenable that persons serving abroad for their country, either as armed forces personnel or as civilians, should be so penalized and I am particularly pleased to include this amendment with Bill C-62 today.
Another significant provision is the one which gives to the Minister of National Health and Welfare authority to declare overpayments uncollectable in order to ease financial hardships. We all know how easy it is to make minor mistakes in calculations-

Here are three other aspects of the bill: any provincial benefit payable under the provisions of the Old Age Security Act may be added to the OAS pension cheque, subject to an agreement between the province concerned and the federal administration. In such case, every three months the provincial government would reimburse to the federal government the costs arising out of that agreement. Such an agreement already exists with Prince Edward Island where family allowances are included every month in the federal government's allowance cheque.
The Old Age Security Fund will be eliminated and the benefits will be taken directly out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. At the present time, there is no money left in the Old Age Security Fund and the deficits have therefore been made up through temporary loans from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. With the implementation of fiscal reforms in 1971, the former tax rates relative to old age security, 4 per cent on personal income, 3 per cent on corporate income and 3 per cent on sales, were united within the regular tax structure and tied up at those levels. There now exists no means to increase those rates to replenish the Old Age Security Fund. The present act stipulates that the fund must reimburse loans made out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, without however, providing any source of revenue to make such reimbursement. To remedy the situation, the OAS Fund will be eliminated and all benefits under the legislation will be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
Finally, the Old Age Assistance Act will be repealed. The act provided for the payment of an allowance, subject to a means test, to persons 65 to 70 years old. The program was administered by the provinces and the federal government took part in its financing. The act has been inoperative since 1969 as a result of amendments to the OAS Act that reduced the age of eligibility for the pension from 70 to 65 between 1966 and 1970, which reduction gradually eliminated the Old Age Assistance Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member had been in attendance earlier, he would have heard one of his colleagues refer to the same matter. The reason many members of this party are not here is that our caucus is meeting in Halifax to determine policies as alternatives to the rotten policies this country faces under this government.
I understand that the minister wishes this bill to pass today. I have a piece of advice to give him. If he wants it to pass today, he should sit over there, read his mail and be quiet while I make my observations. I mentioned a little earlier the policy of this government in respect of hiring outside consultants and its other policies involving OFY, LIP, unemployment insurance, and so on. Yet it has the unmitigated gall to bring in a bill which excludes widows, widowers, spinsters, bachelors and divorced persons. It would certainly seem to me that this government is mixed up fn its priorities.
We will let this bill go through. We certainly shall not vote against it. But we would like to know what are the priorities of this government. We feel this bill is unjust, illogical and discriminatory. It shows that this government has callously forgotten the great contribution our senior citizens have made to the development of this country. The government has forgotten that the need of these people who have been excluded is just as important as the need of others, and should be recognized.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for about half my life-and I am afraid that is literally true-I have been in the position of having to deal with proposals regarding old age pensions which fail to go far enough but which are steps in the right direction. It has always been my practice to point out the shortcomings and deficiencies, but nevertheless to vote for and give my support to anything that represents progress. That, sir, will be my position again today. I shall in fact be pointing out some of the shortcomings and deficiencies of Bill C-62, but it is a step in the direction I want us to move and I intend to give it my support, and I hope that it will be possible for us to give this bill second reading this afternoon and to refer it to the standing committee where it can be studied carefully.
It was my intention to deal directly with the bill and some of the things that were said about it this morning by the minister. In other words, I did not intend to comment on any speeches that might be made between the time the minister had the floor and the time I got it. I must say, however, that some of the things that were said by my good friend from Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) prompt me to give him two or three minutes.
I happen to agree with him strongly and forcefully that this bill is discriminatory in that it provides pensions for only a limited number of persons betwe _>n age 60 and age 65. It is discriminatory in that it forgets spinsters, widows, bachelors and widowers. I think anyone who has followed the old age pension debates will confirm that throughout the piece I have argued, not just for the payment of pensions to spouses but for lowering the eligibility age and for making the only test below age 65 whether or not one is in the labour market. I contend, therefore, that I have every right to stand today and complain about this bill.
Old Age Security Act
I find it difficult, however, to sit and listen to the complaints of my friend from Hamilton West in view of the fact that the bill follows exactly the principle his party advocated in the last election campaign.

speechtext: We know your name.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR
speechtext:
I have in my hand a copy of a Conservative Party commitment to old age pensioners that has on it the picture of Robert Stanfield-"the one who cares". This particular Conservative Party campaign leaflet from the last election is devoted entirely to what the Conservative Party would do for the pensioners. Listen to this sentence:
We will ensure that the wife or husband of a pensioner aged 65 or more becomes eligible for the old age security and guaranteed income benefits at 55, if he or she is not employed.
There are two differences between that sentence and the bill now before us. One is that the spouse's pension should begin at 55 instead of 60. The other difference is that the Progressive Conservatives made no reference to marital relations other than those that are strictly legal. But that sentence and the position of the Progressive Conservative Party throughout these discussions has been one that has ignored the spinsters, the widows, the bachelors and the widowers.
The Progressive Conservatives never argued for paying a pension to everyone in the lower age brackets. Their position was that they would pay it to the spouse of a pensioner; in other words, the spouse of one already 65 or over. I point out that earlier in this session, on one or more occasions, the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Mac-quarrie) welcomed the proposal being advanced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and urged the minister to bring it in soon and make it effective earlier. There is such a thing as standing by what you have stood for. The Progressive Conservatives have asked, in principle, for the very thing the minister has brought in today. Why, then, does my friend, the hon. member for Hamilton West, spend half of his speech condemning the very thing in this bill that the Progressive Conservatives have endorsed?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR
speechtext:
Lest anyone think I did not take the precaution to look up our own election literature to see whether we had made that mistake-I was sure we had not, because I usually have something to say about our pension policy-this is what we said in our election literature for 1974:
We must... make old age security pensions and Canada Pension Plan benefits available to all who are voluntarily off the labour market after reaching the age of sixty.
We did not limit the pensions we should pay to those below the age of 65 who meet a marriage test. The Progressive Conservatives did, the Liberals do, so why do the two of them have to fight about it? I said I would give my hon.

June 6, 1975
Old Age Security Act
friend two or three minutes and now I think we had better get back to the bill.
I welcome any progress in the field of old age pensions. As I said earlier, I have been arguing for a long time- about half my life-for improvements of this kind, and I dearly want to see pensions paid to all those who are 60 and are out of the labour market. Therefore, when a bill comes in that pays it to some persons at the age of 60, I will support it. But it is discriminatory along the very lines that the hon. member for Hamilton West has pointed out.
The figures I have been able to collect-perhaps they are subject to correction, but I am sure they are not very far out-are that there are about 770,000 Canadians between the ages of 60 and 65. I understand that this bill will provide pensions to about 85,000 of those 770,000. That leaves 685,000 Canadians between the ages of 60 and 65 who will not qualify under this bill. That includes many single persons, be they spinsters, widows, bachelors, widowers or persons who are divorced, and there is no doubt in the world that many of those single persons, particularly single women, are in greater need than many of those who happen to have spouses. For the government at this time to say no to all of those others is, I think, most unfair.
I do not intend to spend any time on the points raised by my friends to my right about the provisions for spouses' pensions in the case of common law relationships. I am not shocked by this. This kind of provision is in a number of pieces of our legislation. But I do think it is a bit hard to take when a single woman between 60 and 65 cannot have a pension, whereas some other woman who is living common law can have the pension.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR
speechtext: I wish the government would make up its mind what it wants to encourage in terms of marital relations. It goes both ways. Let us take the case where both man and wife are over 65: each of them would get more if they separated, because the total under OAS and GIS for a couple is less than twice that for a single person. So in that area the government is encouraging married couples over 65 to break up so that they get a little more. On the other hand, they are saying to single persons between 60 and 65, "If you want a pension, shack up with somebody over 65 who has a pension".

speechtext: Such things from you, Stanley, on a Friday! You will have to move from our street.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR
speechtext:
The sense of shock being displayed around here is somewhat synthetic. My point is that this is an example of the unfairness of this piece of legislation. I urge very strongly that the government consider more seriously the position of those who are single, whether they be spinsters, widows, bachelors, widowers or divorced persons, and that they should

be covered by this legislation. Again I say that in so far as it goes, it is good. For the first time we will be paying pensions under the Old Age Security Act to some persons who are below 65 years of age.
I have been here long enough and I have seen enough progress in old age security legislation to know that it is only a matter of time until 60 will be the pensionable age under both old age security legislation and the Canada Pension Plan. But why do we have to wait for it so long? Why do we have to make so many speeches? Why do we have to have so many elections to get progress in a direction that is clearly one we all want to take? So in the name of the 685,000 Canadians between the ages of 60 and 65 who will not be covered by this bill, I plead that when we get into committee the minister will give serious consideration to improving the bill to cover them all.
I also welcome the references made this morning by my friend, the hon. member for Hamilton West, to the further departure from universality that is involved in this bill. It is not the first departure, as I thought he was suggesting this morning, because the guaranteed income supplement is already a case of non-universality. In this bill we are moving, as I say, into the 60 to 65 area but we are applying, again, a means test-the government calls it an income test-which will mean that many of these people will not get the pension. Indeed, this is going to come as a shock to many couples. The minister can say it is the same income test that applies to two persons both of whom are over 65, but in my view he is wrong there as well. I listened with great interest to the minister's efforts this morning to tell us how great is the history of the Liberal Party in terms of pensions.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR
speechtext:
I have lived through most of that history. In fact, my colleagues and I have had a good deal to do with prompting or provoking Liberal governments to move in the direction of better pensions. I notice that the ministers moved rather quickly over the point at which the government, having finally accepted universality, when back to so-called selectivity.
That is another thing that I do not like about this bill; it is that it provides a further move away from the principle of universality. So I call, again, for pensions for all persons who are 60 years of age and not yet 65 who are out of the labour market. I believe in universality; therefore I do not like means tests or income tests, but I understand them. They have been applied to persons over 65. They are applied to persons under the War Veterans Allowance Act. They have been applied under other legislation in the past and they are part of our social fabric.
I understand work tests as well. We had one for a number of years under the Canada Pension Plan and I would be happy to have one that would apply between 60 and 65. But this marriage test is something new in social legislation. One receives the pension not because of age or need but because it can be shown that one is married to someone who is of pensionable age. It is a departure which I think is a mistake.
June 6, 1975

I know that many people in this House, including many Progressive Conservatives, have called for pensions for spouses for a long time. I think that we have been asking for the right thing in our insistence that it should be a pension based on age, and that in the case of those who are 60 but not yet 65 the only test should be whether they are in the labour market.
While I am on my feet, there are two or three other things I should like to call for with regard to pensions; then I would like to comment on some of the things in the bill other than its main provision for spouses' pensions. On a Friday morning two or three weeks ago I tried to present a motion under Standing Order 43. Oddly enough, it did not receive the necessary unanimous consent. However, I came right out and proposed that it was time to raise the basic old age security pension to $300 a month. I make this plea again this afternoon. Some may think it is a bit high, but I can remember when I was told I was asking too much when I asked for $30 per month.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR
speechtext: But I suggest that with inflation running as it is, with the principle of universality being still much better than the principle of selectivity, and with all the other increases this House has passed for those on high salaries, this is what we ought to be going for, a pension of $300 per month across the board. Let it take the place of the guaranteed income supplement, and let us achieve some of that equality the Minister of National Health and Welfare talks about in his speeches before various service clubs and some of that equality he talked about in this House when he was presenting Bill C-16.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) is saying some-
Old Age Security Act
thing very nice; but these things came about with the backing of my colleagues, my party and the people across the country who believe in this sort of thing.

speechtext: Where are your colleagues?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR
speechtext:
There is something else which is not in this bill and which ought to be there. I refer to the escalation formula. The minister hardly ever makes a speech in which he does not boast of the fact that old age security pensions and guaranteed income supplement payments are escalated according to the rise in the cost of living, and that they are now escalated quarterly instead of annually. As I have pointed out times without number, that is an escalation which is always several months behind, so that pensioners never receive the increase when they need it to meet the current increase in the cost of living. In this age of computers and that sort of thing, it would not be impossible to provide escalation on a current basis and I feel very strongly that that should be done.
Something else which is long overdue in the Old Age Security Act has to do with the position of people who come to this country, and Canadians who leave this country and go elsewhere. We have a rather strange rule about old age security. One either receives all of it or none of it. If one is here at age 55 and stays until age 65, one receives all of it; but one might live here from birth until age 55 or 56, go somewhere else and not receive the pension at all. There are problems with regard to people who move from one country to another. It is time there was some kind of formula which would involve reciprocity between this country and others so that wherever people move or live they will receive the best possible pension.
I am not asking for the rules to be changed so that individuals can receive two full pensions from two separate countries. That happens now in some cases. But as opposed to those who manage to obtain full old age security in Canada and full social security in the United States, there are others who get lost between two stools and do not receive either. I mention this because, as the minister knows, I asked him one day in the standing committee whether he would put his high-powered research people to work on this question, and he was happy to tell me that he had already done so and there was some hope that something in this line might be done in this session. He told us the last time this matter came up in committee that it would not be in Bill C-62. I regret that, but I push for proper provisions so that people do not lose their pensions entirely because they came here too late, or do not lose their Canadian pensions because for family, health or other reasons they go somewhere else to live.
I am proud of what we have done with old age security. We have made tremendous improvements. We have taken care of many of these details, but that is no reason for us to stop when, as we move along, we still further improvements we could make.
Mr. Speaker, I said that in addition to the things I wanted to call for today I would like to comment briefly on some of the other things this bill does I welcome the

June 6, 1975
Old Age Security Act
provision in the bill which will allow absence from Canada to be counted as presence here in the case of persons serving in the armed forces, or doing certain other things abroad, when it comes to making up for time they lost in trying to qualify for old age security. This is a matter which has been debated in the House several times, and a private member's resolution by one of the Progressive Conservatives on this matter was passed. It probably does not cover a great many people, but it is an unfairness which is being corrected by this bill and I am glad that is being done.
I am interested in the provision which will make it possible for provincial pension supplements to be included in the federal old age security cheque. In these days, when banks are increasing their charges and charging people every time they write a cheque, make a deposit or walk in or out of the bank, I think it is a good ideal to reduce the number of cheques old age pensioners have to handle, so long as there is no reduction in the total amount. I believe this is an appropriate change. I assume it is up to the provinces whether they include in their agreement with the federal government some arrangement under which the name of the province appears on the cheque as well. I can hardly imagine any province letting Ottawa write the cheque and claim it is a federal cheque without the name of the province appearing there with it. I think this is a commendable move.
It also sets out in this bill that the minister will have the authority to cancel uncollectable debts in those cases where hardship would ensue and where the mistake that was made, whether by the pensioner or the department, was clearly unintentional.
Then I come to what might seem just a clean-up matter in this bill, but it is one thing that I welcome as warmly as I can. It will make no monetary difference at the moment, but in principle it is terribly important. I refer to the fact that the old age security fund is being wiped out and any reference to any special tax, whether direct or by transfer from the Department of National Revenue to the old age security fund, is being done away with. The minister explained in his press release and again this morning that this change is being made because it has become mathematically or administratively impossible to keep up with the changes. In my view, it is more than that.
When we first considered the Old Age Security Act-a committee recommended it in 1950, the bill was brought in in 1951 and it became law on January 1, 1952-when we first brought it in, it was such a far reaching proposal, to pay pensions to everyone aged 70 and over, as was the case then, that in order to sell the idea we had to put on this special tax, and establish a special fund. We had a 2-2-2 tax in those days for the special fund and after a time this tax went up a bit.
What did it mean, Mr. Speaker? If the fund was short, the minister of finance, by law, had to lend money to it so that pensioners could be paid. If the fund was in surplus, we tried to argue that some of the surplus should be used for an increase in pensions but we were told it could not be done and we had to follow the act. It really had no meaning. Those taxes were a regressive form of taxation

which meant that the wealthy person paid the same amount as the person who did not earn very much.
We have done away with that and are finalizing it in this bill. We now say that old age pensions are paid in their entirety out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund; in other words, the total cost of old age pensions is coming out of the fund which gets its resources on the basis of ability to pay. This means that those with greater incomes pay more toward old age security than those with little or no income. Although this may seem like a technical or administrative change, it is an important one.
The other day I was reading a book on the history of pensions. I noticed that the author referred to this regressive type of taxation and expressed the hope that some day it would be done away with. It has been done away with in this bill. We are establishing the fact that old age pensions are a matter of right because people who reach pensionable age are part of our society and have played their part in building up the economy. No special tax is necessary, therefore, or no special fund is necessary to operate the whole proposition.
I point out also-and I want to come back and say something about both of these changes-that this bill abolishes the Old Age Assistance Act. It has been dead for a number of years, anyway. This act was introduced in 1951 to provide for pensions between ages 65 and 70 on a means test basis, paid partly by Ottawa and partly by the provinces. That has been replaced by old age security being paid at age 65, so there is no point in keeping that statute on the books any longer.
I hope you will pardon me for going back to what some of us have said in the past, Mr. Speaker, but in 1950 and 1951 we wanted the pension to be paid at age 65 on a universal basis, and we wanted it paid out of consolidated revenue and not on the basis of a special tax. We wanted it to be paid as a matter of right. It has taken us a long time to get that principle through but we are getting there by this bill. I think there is a moral to that. If one can be here for a few years and see that some of the things one has stood and fought for, because they are right, have been accepted, then one can hope that the same thing will happen again.
Just as we wrote our old age security fund into the act to sell the idea of getting it started, I hope that today, when we are putting in pensions at 60 on a limited basis only for spouses, it is just the beginning too. I hope it will not be very long until some of us can stand in this House and say we have won that point as well-that we have pensions across the board at age 60 for all those who are out of the labour market.
I welcome this opportunity to give my support to this bill, Mr. Speaker. I do so without question. I shall be voting for it and in committee I shall be supporting it. I hope we can get it through soon so that the 80,000-odd people who would benefit by it in October will have no doubt about it. However, I hope it has been evident that my greater concern at this time is to point out the things that are yet to be done.
We have come a long way since I stood in my place in the back row and pleaded for the pension to go up to $30 a month and for the means test to be removed. Today we are
June 6, 1975

paying $125 or so across the board to everyone aged 65 or over, we are paying over $200 a month to those individuals who get the full supplement, and we are paying over $400 a month to a couple, both of whom are on the supplement. In some of the provinces the pensions are even higher, but with inflation running as it is and with it being established that our people have not only the right to keep up with the cost of living but to share in the standard of living, and with the increased productivity of our country, I contend the time has come for us to talk in terms of pensions across the board of $300 a month.
To get back to this bill, Mr. Speaker, I also contend that the time has come to pay pensions, not just to spouses between ages 60 and 65 but to all people between ages 60 and 65 provided they meet just one test-that they are out of the labour market. That would cover all the people this bill covers, but it would also cover the spinsters, widows, bachelors and widowers, those who never married or are no longer married. I contend that the complaints that these people will be making in the months and years ahead-I hope it is only months, and not years-will be more than justified.
The hon. member of Hamilton West and one of my friends further down the aisle dealt with this matter in a question the other day and raised one point which I think really brings this bill to the test. Take the case of a woman aged 62 who is married to a man aged 65 or over. They have no income, so they qualify for the double pension. Next year he dies, when she is 63. What happens to the woman then? Is the Government of Canada going to be so inhuman as to take away the pension she was getting?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR

My hon. friend is correct; under this bill the government will have to take it away. I suppose it will say it will have to take it away because if it did not, one widow would be getting it while thousands of other widows would not. I submit that test by itself shows that the thinking about this bill has not been adequate and that we need to make real improvements when we get it into committee.
Mr. Speaker, I welcome any bill that moves in the right direction, and this one does. I also welcome the opportunity to argue for further improvements in our old age pension legislation so that we may soon reach the day when our senior citizens have the rights and security to which they are entitled.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF SPOUSE'S ALLOWANCE TO PERSONS SIXTY TO SIXTY-FOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I want to take part in this debate on Bill C-62, a bill we had been awaiting impatiently because we had noted that the government-the Liberal party rather-had promised as early as during the last election campaign of 1974 that this legislation would be passed as soon as the Liberal party would be reelected. Well, Mr. Speaker, this legislation will be implemented only a year and a half after the Liberal party's reelection. So, the
Old Age Security Act
minister should not be surprised if during its consideration either in committee or on second reading amendments are introduced to implement that election promise made by the Liberal party in 1974.
There is another point that was just raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), namely the case of those people who would momentarily be covered by this bill, that is spouses between the ages of 60 and 65. In the event the older spouse should die-a question raised by my colleague from Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) a few days ago-the younger spouse would automatically be disentitled to his or her pension. That is another subject on which we are considering moving an amendment to improve this bill.
Generally speaking, the principle of the bill is quite acceptable, and I am one of the first to welcome it since as early as 1966 I was I think the first member in the history of Canadian parliamentarism to place a motion on the order paper of this House asking precisely that the spouse receive the pension, no matter what the age.
In every ensuing session I tabled the same motion since I was not entitled to introduce a bill to that effect and I had the opportunity a few times to debate that motion during private members' hour. On every occasion, as strange as it seems, government members always opposed such a move saying that it was nonsense, that it was going to be extremely expensive, that the people of Canada could not afford such a luxury. And still, on the last occasion, March 24, 1975, there was a perceptible change in attitude since at that time the government had already made public its intention of implementing this bill.
Now that this bill is being introduced, Liberal members and the government all agree. And that measure no longer is nonsense, on the contrary it makes sense. Just have a look at the memo or release which was handed to us on June 3, which says that, for instance, this new bill might benefit from 65,000 to 90,000 spouses. You will admit it makes quite a difference whether it is 65,000 or 90,000 spouses. Apparently, the department officials were unable to come up with a more precise figure. And yet, when costs are mentioned, they are said to amount to $100 million. Therefore, whether the number of spouses who will qualify is 65,000 or 90,000, the overall cost will be $100 million.
So I do not quite understand the figures of the minister's officials which leave such a wide gap between the estimate of the number of spouses who might qualify under the new act and the estimate of the costs. I think this calls for some explanation.
Mr. Speaker, the Social Credit Party has long called for improvements to the Old Age Security Act. In his statement this morning, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) said that when only one of the spouses is in receipt of the Old Age Security Pension, they have financial problems, and his attention was drawn many times to that.
And indeed we drew his attention to that problem many times. On December 3, 1974,1 once again raised that matter in this House on the occasion of a debate on the business of supply, and I proposed:
That this House regrets that the government neglected to make all those who reached the age of 60, as well as their spouses although such

June 6, 1975
Old Age Security Act
spouses may not have reached pensionable age, eligible for the Old Age Pension.
Once again, the motion was negatived, and even a representative of the Liberal party, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, said:
Mr. Speaker, today I speak on behalf of the government against the motion proposed by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) who has advocated that the old age security pension be given to any person who has reached the age of 60, as well as to the spouse even if the spouse has not reached pensionable age.
Now, Mr. Speaker, is it not a bit strange that hardly a few months ago they would have nothing to do with it, and today they are accepting that proposal. Of course we are extremely pleased that they do. But as I mentioned earlier, even if we have reasons to be satisfied with the principle of that bill, there nevertheless remains some obscure points which will have to be made clearer. The Social Credit Party has long claimed that the Old Age Pension should be granted anyone over 60. When I say anyone, I have reasons to say, as Social Credit and other hon. members in fact did, that the inquiries made with respect to applications of old people respecting their pension should be withheld. I believe that principle should apply to every field, whether social security or other fields of social welfare now available.
When the Guaranteed Income Supplement Act, added to the Old Age Security Act, was discussed in 1966, and I have here the Hansard for December 5, 1966, the then Minister of National Health and Welfare stated the following when introducing the bill, as reported on page 10711:
In some instances the pensioner may wish to revise his initial statement of income because of more detailed information obtained later. If this is done, an adjustment of the supplement will be made to take into account this change. Information supplied on income can be checked against income tax returns and third party information supplied to the Department of National Revenue on T-3, T-4, T-5 and other returns.
That, Mr. Speaker, is all the mystery behind the investigation system imposed upon older citizens applying for the guaranteed income supplement. We all know the difficulties experienced by the aged, especially during the spring when they must file the famous guaranteed income supplement application form. This was especially true last spring, with the total mess of the post office and letters accumulating at the Montreal postal centre. In my constituency, pensioners filled up to three forms that were left about on some counter. Without the competency and good will shown by the Quebec old age security office director, Mr. Turbide, a very understanding gentleman, I believe some of our older citizens would have lost their guaranteed income supplement.
I intervened each time and was so able to have the supplement reinstated at the right level, but at the cost of numerous complications and fears for those concerned, who do not know which way to turn when the time comes to have the supplement accepted.

to take the card away. But with the present system, everything has to be done anew each year, and even a number of times each year as is often the case, in order to check whether a pensioner's revenue status changed.
What is even worse, when a person applies in mid-year, a projected income statement is required. As it is rather difficult to project one's revenues, errors will happen. The OAS director advises the pensioner that due to his first declaration being inaccurate, an overpayment must be repaid.
To my great pleasure, the minister recognized the big difficulties that exist and will try to eliminate them in the future. I hope I did not mistakenly understand that the provision the minister dealt with will apply not only to the spouse not yet 65 years old, but to any old age security applicant.
Mr. Speaker, if we abolished the present test, we would at the same time free those who apply for the old age security from many worries and headaches.

The particular point the hon. member for Hamilton West brought out was the fact that this bill does suggest we are only paying attention to the spouses and, of necessity, unmarried spouses. But I do not think that is particularly true. I think we should not fall into that danger. We should remember compassion and the compassion this government has shown all along for those who are in need.
I think the Old Age Security Act, with this income test and allowance, is a guaranteed minimum for the level of income that we want to reach particularly in this group. I might remind the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that if these two people had nothing at all they would start out with $408, and that is considerable, considering that they now have nothing. I think that in this group, and in the group he particularly alluded to, the danger arises in the area of the spinster, the widower, the bachelor, the single person, the lonely person, the person who has nobody to lean on, no crutch, no assistance at all at this age level. The latter, particularly, might become a victim of early retirement, and I think we have to be very careful of the early retirement situation to which this could lead.
Early retirement has a ring to it for hard-working Canadians during moments of heavy job pressure, and it
Old Age Security Act
may sound like the promised land. But the visions of pleasant leisure have proven mirages to many people who have had to face the many problems that retirement brings.
One crucial factor which must be taken into account in deciding the lower age of eligibility for government pensions under Old Age Security or the Canada Pension Plan is the effect this may have on the mandatory retirement age in the general work force. Certainly the last lowering of the age from 70 to 65 drastically reduced labour force participation by people over 65 by one third.
When such earlier retirement is voluntary this is one matter, although as will be seen not all who voluntarily retire wish to remain in retirement, especially after a year or two. But when retirement is involuntary, when it becomes automatic at a certain age regardless of a worker's wishes to stay on, then the question becomes more complex. Is it desirable to move toward a lower eligibility age, which may drastically affect the normal retirement age throughout the economy, before the desire for and the capacity to live with early retirement are determined for the working population aged from 55 to 65?
I am reminded that this may come quickly. Today my secretary turned 50 and pretty soon she will be up to that 55 to 60 bracket, and while not being able to wish her a happy birthday from this seat we wish her well and know she will eventually, as the mother of eight, go into retirement, and to a good one. Happily she will know the government is looking after her retirement, and that people like her will be looked after the same way.
It is not inconceivable that employers could use the availability of government pensions to get rid of older workers they feel are redundant or less than fully productive; they could ensure that these people could qualify for the government pension by the simple expedient of removing them from the labour force or by firing them. Yet these men and women may have no wish to leave work at all. Many people do wish to continue working until they are 65, as can be seen in many instances. For example, despite the excellent pension plan available to qualified federal government employees who retire before the age of 65, only about 15 per cent of those eligible exercise their option to do so.
Aside from the effects of early retirement on the workers themselves, there is also the general economic impact to consider. Even if almost all retirements are voluntary, what would happen if due to the impact of lowering the old age security and the Canada Pension Plan eligibility age, a large number of highly skilled and highly productive workers decided to leave their jobs? We must not underestimate our older workers. Less and less work is manual where the premium is on youth and on strength. Speaking of youth, I know of somebody else who is going into retirement tomorrow. When the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemount (Mr. Lachance) goes up to the altar and takes unto himself a bride. I think he is to be congratulated.

speechtext:
I thought that today's was a $700 or $800 speech. I thought it was one of the better ones his writers had provided him with, and I hope I do not create sfny dissension among his speechwriters if I suggest that he should go up to $700 or $800 for that one. This bill appears to me to be partly written by speechwriters. As for the other part, it looks as if he has given a different page to each section of his department and said, "Write the page and pay no attention to what the other pages say; we will put it together and throw it in front of parliament".
This bill is one of the most confusing and contradictory pieces of paper ever put in front of us, and perhaps I can point to some of the contradictions.
The definition of a spouse is the first thing that creates concern and puzzlement. The first page clearly defines the meaning of "spouse". It says:
"spouse" in relation to a pensioner includes a person of the opposite sex who has lived with the pensioner for three or more years where there is a bar to their marriage or at least one year where there is no such bar and the pensioner and that person have publicly represented themselves as man and wife;
That sounds quite simple, except for the fact that one of the minister's speechwriters put out a news release the same day saying that persons applying for the guaranteed income supplement and spouse's allowance for the first time will be required to submit a certificate of marriage. There is no way on earth that you can have both of those things, and I say that a bill of parliament should take precedence over the minister's press release. So when we come to consider the meaning of "spouse" we will take it
June 6, 1975

that it means what the bill says it means, not what his hired speechwriters and pressmen say.
Page three of the bill talks of separation. This is part of my general complaint about the bill-it is such a mean bill. It is a mean, small-minded bill that goes out of its way to see where it can cut people out. Under the side-note "Eligible spouse of pensioner" the bill provides:
For the purposes of this Part, a spouse of a pensioner is an eligible spouse if the spouse
(a) is not separated from the pensioner;
What makes the minister think that a person will not need an allowance if they are separated from their partner? It is obvious that they will need money more than if they were both living together. Perhaps the minister is trying to keep families together and is saying they will suffer a financial loss if they separate. I believe that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was on the right wicket when he said that the government has no business in the bedrooms of the nation. Yet here is the minister insisting that in order to retain their allowance they must continue to live together even if there are several reasons why they should not.
Clause 5 has an explanatory note, and there we find a definition that is different from the definition of "spouse". This note reads:
The purpose of this amendment is to provide after September 1975 for the payment of spouse's allowances to persons 60 to 64 inclusive who are married to and living with pensioners.
The phrase used there is "married to", yet according to the definition of "spouse" they do not have to be married. In fact it is clearly spelt out how they are to be treated if they are not married.
On page four of the bill there is a residence requirement. While I am pleased about some of the things said about residence requirements in the speech of the minister, quite a bit of this is due to the prodding and the unbelievable success of the Conservative member for Okanagan-Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) in getting a resolution through this House providing that service in the armed forces of Canada overseas would be counted as residence in Canada. The bill provides that a person is eligible if he-
-has resided in Canada after attaining eighteen years of age and prior to the day on which the application is approved for an aggregate period of at least forty years.
In other words, a person who is 18 has to reside in Canada another 40 years, which takes him to the age of 58, allowing him only two years out of Canada. That is very little time, and I suggest many of us spend two years out of Canada on holidays during a lifetime.
The minister listed several exempted categories this morning, including servicemen and people in government service. But there was one category he missed, and I hope it is an omission that can be corrected in committee. I refer to students. Students often spend two years outside Canada. If they are 18 and they go to a post-graduate school in the United States or elswhere for three years, when they reach 60 they will discover they do not qualify because they will not have an aggregate period in Canada of 40 years. I think the minister should exempt students along with the others he mentioned.
Old Age Security Act
The bill also provides that there must be a joint application for a spouse's allowance. It is not every couple that will sign a joint application, and I fail to see why there must be a joint application. The assumption is that the couple are getting along well together and are not on opposite sides of the house refraining from co-habitation. It seems to me that this is an invitation to a pensioner to withhold the allowance from his spouse if he feels mean enough.
There is a provision on page 5 that hits widows above all others. I refer to the cessation of allowance provision. This applies to those who cease to be a spouse or an eligible spouse. Most speakers today have mentioned the case of the woman of 62 who has a husband who is 66, each of whom draws half of the pension. Then the husband dies, and suddenly all of the pension ceases and the widow is left destitute. This seems to me to be about as mean as you can get with government money, particularly when spent the way this government spends it.
Then on page six of the bill provision is made for a means test. Speaking for myself, I am one of those who have never believed that a means test is necessary. It is a disincentive to people to prepare for their old age. It is a disincentive to save. It is also a disincentive for those who are in a pension plan. I suggest it only exaggerates the current problem.
If a couple are in middle age, 45 and 40, and they look forward to the day when they will be 65 and 60, at the present time they will get $400 a month, or a little more, if they arrive at those ages penniless, having made no preparation for their retirement. If these people have prepared for their old age they will receive from the government $100 a month, or one-quarter of the money they would otherwise receive. They will be making a sacrifice if they prepare for old age to the extent of taking out a private pension plan, or buying into a deferred payment plan or a registered retirement saving's plan, or if they should belong to a union. They can look at the pension and say that the first $300 will be funny money and will not be of any use to them. They can say that if they did not have it they would receive it from the government.
The worker can say that the first $300 of a pension plan is not worth anything to him and that the plan should start above that point so that it would be a good pension. I think we will end up with more people taking the view that it would be stupid to arrive at retirement age with any income, because otherwise they would receive $400 a month. I think this is bad for the country especially at a time when it is hoped that we can buy back our own industry from a foreign country.
There is one final point I should like to make concerning the cancellation of the Old Age Assistance Act which is being repealed by this legislation. This concerns me. I am not a lawyer, but I notice that in the original Old Age Assistance Act it states that payments to a province pursuant to this section-referring to Section 3-shall be made only in respect of a recipient who fulfils certain conditions.
Section 3(2) (c) of the Old Age Assistance Act refers to an unmarried person whose income, inclusive of assist-
29561 - 69)4

June 6, 1975
Old Age Security Act
ance, is not more than $1,260 a year. If the Old Age Assistance Act is cancelled it seems to me this would mean we would be taking away the rights with regard to unmarried persons. Since this bill does not refer to unmarried persons it would seem that some people will lose out.
Section 7 of the Old Age Assistance Act states that in every agreement the province shall, subject to section 3, specify the minimum age of a recipient and any other conditions of eligibility set forth in the provincial law. I should like to give credit to the government of the province of British Columbia for its thinking in this regard. It has specified the minimum age of a recipient at below age 65. It would seem to me that by cancelling the Old Age Assistance Act we may be cancelling the provision which enables the provinces to pay pensions to people under age 65 and have the federal government share in this.
I hope that this matter will be discussed in the committee so that I may be reassured no harm will be done by the cancellation of the Old Age Assistance Act. I am more reassured when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) tells me that it will not hurt anyone than I am by the press releases of the federal government at this time.
I shall not take any more of the time of the House because I realize other members wish to speak. I, like others who have spoken, will support this bill because it covers 80,000 people in need. I think the faults in the bill are obvious to all members. A re-writing of the bill would seem to be necessary. We will support the bill at this stage in the hope that it will come back from the committee in an improved state.

When his mind makes appointments that his body can't keep.
I do not know in what category of that poem the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre might fall, but he is a man who has brought great distinction to this House. I am glad he has had the advantage of reading the literature produced by the Progressive Conservative party during the last election, because there was in that literature a commitment to something that goes far beyond this particular legislation. I am sure we all agree that parliaments must deal with the pieces of legislation they have before them. This is an inadequate piece of legislation for many Canadians. It discriminates, as many members have said, against the large group of Canadians who perhaps finds themselves, in terms of their ability to make a place for themselves in the work force, in a worse position than others. However, that is the extent of the government's commitment with regard to old age security at this time. I do not know how else to measure the commitment of a government than by looking at the legislation that is bfought before us. If this is the extent, and I think it is at this time, of the government's commitment, then I think it is inadequate.
Although we intend to support the legislation on the same basis as does the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that is, on the basis that it is a small step forward, we cannot support it without bringing forth questions-it would be dishonest for us to merely say, yes, we support the bill-in terms of that group of people in Canada whom the bill does not affect, such as single women, widows, widowers, bachelors and divorced persons. I know there are federal-provincial problems. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) said that applying the provisions of this legislation to the above mentioned group of people is a long way away, if it is to come at all.
The liberal government has the habit of trotting out some things on a four year basis in terms of advance notice. I do not know why they do that, and the beauty of this Friday afternoon does not allow me to be cynical, but the fact of the matter is that this legislation is only worthy of support to the extent that it goes. It should not be built into something that it is not, and I hope that if necessity speeded us into an election perhaps we could find ourselves dealing with those categories of people who have been left out from this legislation.
The other matter dealt with by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in terms of the literature to which
June 6, 1975

he referred for our edification, and I am glad he did, was that the Liberal party's commitment on July 8, 1974, only dealt with married people. That is quite so, it did. What concerns me about this legislation is not so much the relationships that it envisages-and I am sure the committee will unscramble anything that has to be unscrambled-as the fact that it is given predominance in the legislation ahead of a group of people who, in terms of our economic life today, need some protection within the context of this bill, however limited it may be. I am referring to married couples who depend upon this type of payment for their existence.
If a priority is established, then it should be in favour of married couples because it was in that sense that the piece of literature with which we dealt at some length was phrased. Married couples should receive first priority within the context of this legislation, and they should not be sacrificed for others who might be qualified on a different basis.
Now I want to deal with one matter which, I am happy to say, is dealt with in the bill. It has to do with financial errors. I have written to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) on many occasions regarding problems of overpayment of pensions. I must say to the minister that he has always been very prompt in dealing with the correspondence I have sent to him, and I am sure that is generally the way he has dealt with correspondence from all members of parliament. Perhaps some of his colleagues in cabinet could emulate this. There is an immediate acknowledgement from the minister of letters sent to him, and there is always a follow up. I do not want that practice to change because I mention this today, but he is the one minister for whom it is not necessary to mark one's files to remind the minister to answer. I do not want his head to blow up so much that he will have difficulty getting into the lobby, but that is a statement of fact.
The unfortunate thing about this particular error which this bill is meant to catch, that is, financial error and the necessity of paying back, is that the necessity in law is there. There is absolutely nothing the minister can do in terms of his discretion to assist old age pensioners who find themselves in that position. His answer has always had to be that he is sorry, it was an error, and he apologizes. He can make all the excuses and protestations he wants, but whatever is the computer they use that made the mistake, older people do not necessarily take advantage of that kind of error, and there is nothing the minister can do about it. I have had this experience many times, and I understand that that is the reason for this provision in the bill.
I think it is a very important clause because it allows, in case of senior citizens, that special group of people who in terms of opportunities for advancement might be called disadvantaged, for an exercise of discretion such as other ministers, notably the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), have exercised with respect to ministerial permits in proper cases, and there is a question as to how it operates. I am not suggesting that the minister should be forgiven for errors which cause inconvenience, but I am suggesting that this is a very good provision for which the minister should be commended.
Old Age Security Act
Our party's policy with regard to senior citizens is much more far reaching than is the government's, and it has been for some period of time. It is an expression of our concern for a group of Canadians who fall within a special category, not only because of the difficulties which they experience in the work force and in remaining in the work force in a society which puts increasing emphasis on youth, but because most senior citizens have made a significant contribution to the well-being of the community. They have laid the foundation upon which we advance. For that reason alone I think they are entitled to our consideration.
It is also important that we look at the needs and requirements of senior citizens from another point of view, the need which they have in their particular circumstances to care for themselves in terms of housing, food, and health services, all of which are very important components of the cost price index in this country. It is a fact which I do not think anyone will dispute, that senior citizens spend a larger proportion of their income on these necessities than do other citizens, and it is important therefore that we never lose sight of the necessity for constantly updating and reviewing the amounts of money we are prepared to pay as citizens in a progressive society toward their well-being.
It is important also that we take a look at the cost price index to see whether it is the proper index upon which to gauge their needs and requirements. Some people have spoken of an old persons' index or the index of the disadvantaged, in search of phrases that would be weighted in favour of senior citizens who might find themselves in need, because it is a fact that senior citizens have different needs and expenses than does the average Canadian family of four and, as a result, new measurements must be devised to meet these unique needs.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the other day called for a basic old age pension of $300, and he referred to it again today. I really do not know whether or not the country can afford that, but I believe that whether the figure is $300 or any other figure, a country with our riches in terms of our resources, our gross national product and the opportunities which we are able to give to our young people, and to other people who do not have the disadvantages of senior citizens, should not lose sight of what is in the spirit of the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I believe that senior citizens have to be treated as a special case. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has made a life's work of treating senior citizens' pensions, superannuations and other pensions as special cases. I do not really believe we have tapped the possibilities with respect to aid, not only in terms of monthly cheques, but aid in terms of the provision of adequate housing, in terms of provision of adequate services for those who, perhaps through age, cannot get around as well as they might. There was an instance of this in Ottawa-Carleton not too long ago. I think these have to be considered in a special category.
When I think of the amounts of money the government has been prepared to spend in certain areas and when I

Old Age Security Act
think of the fact that since 1961 the total cost of operating the Privy Council office and the office of the Prime Minister has increased by 1,148 per cent for a total increase of $5,901,000, then I think the government must give more than lip service to the contention that it is its duty to protect the disavantaged in terms of present benefits.
When I hear that the government is prepared to spend $821 million on professional consultant services-that is over and above the very capable public service of this country-and those services have increased 509.1 per cent since 1961-when I hear of that kind of extravangance I am not one of those who believe that we are incapable of providing for our senior citizens a continually increasing adequate income. If we are not prepared to take the steps which are necessary to fight inflation, or in the alternative if we cannot, which seems to be the argument of the government, then the government must recognize its duty to protect these people.
When the present benefits are related to skyrocketing inflation in terms of necessities of life and how those necessities relate to senior citizens as a particular group, I think those figures themselves speak for the necessity, not just for this legislation, but for ending the discrimination which is apparent in the absence of those provisions for other single people-the single woman, the widow, the widower, the bachelor, or the divorced person.
This discrimination cries out for action, and it is in that sense that I think this legislation is inadequate. Let us make no mistake about it. Let us not beat our chests with pride over this legislation. Let us not have the minister put his elbow out of joint from patting himself on the back over this piece of legislation, because in terms of the problem we have really not yet begun, and I do not want to gainsay in any way the efforts of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I believe that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has been in the forefront of this fight. If the government has copied what he has proposed, then as a plagiarist I think it has done a reasonable job. I do want to gainsay that, but I am satisfied that all of the good will toward senior citizens does not rest in the bosom of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. There are many of us on all sides of the House who feel very strongly about this subject. Many of us today feel just a little twinge of guilt when we compare the magnitude of the problem with the relative poverty of the answer in terms of this legislation.
I understand that another hon. member wishes to speak, and I will relinquish the floor. Others have said that we in this party intend to support this legislation. We wish to see it go through today, but I will end by saying that in this particular area our work in this House has really only just begun.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am privileged to take part in this debate, which in my view must rather be a consensus, because there can be nothing but agreement on the objective. This bill is an invitation to make a concrete step to improve the situation of older citizens. It involves a positive gesture, keeping in mind

that there is no perfect solution. What is involved here is the meeting of real and effective needs, through a fair transfer.
We, on the government side, recognize and emphasize that this bill aims at a more adequate treatment, although not perfect. Mr. Speaker, we are much the more pleased that this concern, on the government's part, was one of the objectives set during the last election. We are happy that it can be achieved.
We share real concern on this matter. This is not only an abstract concern, but a deliberate attempt to achieve positive results. We wish to repeat that we are just as much pleased as opposition members with this concensus, if not on the wording or means, at least as a cooperative effort at achieving the aim within the overhall economic situation. In so doing we show consideration for our elders and their vital needs, not being content with what has been done but attempting to do more if a majority so decides.
This is no election time politicking, this is recognizing our obligation to give our older citizens a practical answer to their effective problems.
As a politician concerned with the welfare of all my constituents, I have had an interest in the aged since I headed a home for elder citizens. I also animated Golden Age Clubs. I recognize that elder citizens have special needs, and I cannot accept that they should not have their share. I am inclined to support the minister without reservation on this legislation, no doubt because it incorporates in law the principle of a pension for every person. This in my view is correcting a discrepancy concerning couples in need. In addition to support for the bill, I extend my appreciation to the minister and the government because I regard this as an invitation to make further steps, keeping in sight at all times a constant priority which we should try never to forget.
We must also consider the ability to pay, in other words to redistribute while taking into account the fact that this fight is not and will never be over and that we must have the courage and the ability to fight it when the time comes.
In answer to my colleague from Abitibi (Mr. Laprise), I would say that I consider that government members are and have always been in favour of such a measure. However, we have had tp wait for the right moment to give priority to this concern, and that is a matter of choice and timing. However, we must be sufficiently realistic and honest to understand this and to act accordingly, and also to speak and to listen accordingly. To say this is to be realistic and to take into account the social and economic reality. This is also a challenge to our senior citizens, not to fight and to protest noisily, since there are always too many who do so, but to continue to tell us about their needs in a way that I wish to be energetic and effective, but without losing their serenity and sense of measure.
I would like to speak on behalf of our senior citizens living in sparsely populated areas, which are often forgotten in the total context of our economic reality. Indeed, legislation is too often based on a universal concept, but in the case of Bill C-62, real and special needs are considered, and we may start to hope that our needs will be taken into account.
June 6, 1975

Finally, Bill C-62 provides some authority for the minister. This gives me an opportunity as a new member of Parliament to invite the House to go further and have more confidence in the government. In my opinion, this would add to our seriousness and our effectiveness. I am astounded that some of us act as defenders of our institutions, of the authority of these institutions, and respect nothing when speaking. I am also surprised that the legislation must be such that the statesmen, the representatives of the people, have to sacrifice all their authority in favour of overly powerful public servants. Afterwards, this situation is deplored. We must wonder about this and confirm the credibility of statesmen, their ability to administer and take into account the real needs and the talents of the established authority, as well as their authority and ability to make decisions, and finally, we must confirm the initiative of able individuals, which is too often destroyed by bureaucracy.
And here, I wish to call on all members of the House to regain the required effectiveness of our problem-solving capacity. The question that I ask myself is this: Can we serve Canadians, are we representatives? If so, whom do we represent? Is it possible to represent them? Our people have needs and, because of Bill C-62,1 have the impression not only of being aware of the needs of a certain number of voters, but of giving them a completely practical answer. And I know that members on this side of the House share this feeling and wish to proceed by stages while taking into account the whole political, economic and social reality.
